Lead and hygiene

Most clay cartridges are loaded with lead shot (the small lead pellets inside the cartridge). Lead is a poisonous metal. It builds up in the body, mostly in the bones, and can harm the brain and nerves, the kidneys and the blood. Doctors know of no amount of lead in the body that is completely safe.

Well researched

From the same amount of lead, a child’s body absorbs more than an adult’s, and a growing brain is harmed more easily. In pregnancy, lead stored in the mother’s bones can pass to the unborn child. So children and pregnant women need extra care.

Well researched

At an outdoor shooting ground, much of the lead reaches a shooter through the hands. Lead dust sits on cartridges, empty cases, the cartridge bag, gloves and the gun. From there it gets onto food, a cigarette or the face, and then into the mouth. Some lead is also breathed in, and more of it at indoor ranges.

Some research

Studies of people who shoot at ranges often find raised lead in their blood. Most of this research comes from police, military and other ranges that are not clay grounds, so for clay shooting the picture is less clear.

Some research

The main habit: wash your hands, and your face if you touched it, with soap and water after shooting. Do it before you eat, drink or smoke. Wet wipes help a little but do not replace washing; there are also special wipes made to remove lead.

Some research

Do not eat, drink from open cups or smoke on the stand or while picking up empty cases. Have a snack in the clubhouse or another clean area, with clean hands. Keep your water bottle closed.

Some research

The clothes and shoes you shot in carry lead dust too. Change after shooting and wash shooting clothes separately from the family’s laundry, especially children’s things. Clean your gun in a ventilated place, and wear gloves if you use cleaning chemicals.

Some research

For ordinary training, some shooters choose steel or soft iron shot where the ground and the law allow it. That means less lead around you and in nature. Rules on lead differ between countries and grounds: see Lead, steel and soft iron.

Little research

Tip: If you shoot a lot, are pregnant or planning a pregnancy, or if your child shoots, talk to a doctor. A blood test shows how much lead is in your blood, which mainly reflects recent exposure; a doctor can explain the result.

Well researched

Key points

  • At an outdoor ground much of the lead reaches you through your hands
  • Wash hands and face with soap after shooting and before eating
  • No food, open drinks or smoking on the stand
  • Change after shooting; wash shooting clothes apart from children’s things
  • Shoot a lot, pregnant or a child shooting: talk to a doctor

Did you know?

Lead harms nature too. EU rules ban lead gunshot in and near wetlands: since 15 February 2023, no shot with 1% lead or more in wetlands or within 100 m of them. A wider EU restriction on lead shot is being prepared: see Lead, steel and soft iron.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. At an outdoor ground, how does much of the lead reach a shooter?

    1. Through the skin of the face, from the smoke of each shot
    2. Mainly from drinking tap water at the ground
    3. Through the hands, from cartridges and cases to the mouth
    Answer

    Through the hands, from cartridges and cases to the mouth

    Lead dust moves from cartridges, cases and the gun to the hands, and from the hands to food and the mouth.

  2. Where is a good place for a snack at the ground?

    1. Right on the stand, between your turns
    2. In the clubhouse, after washing your hands
    3. While you pick up your empty cases
    Answer

    In the clubhouse, after washing your hands

    Eat away from the stand and only with clean hands.

  3. How can you check your lead exposure?

    1. With a blood test arranged by a doctor
    2. From the colour of your fingernails
    3. It cannot be measured at all
    Answer

    With a blood test arranged by a doctor

    A blood test shows how much lead is in your blood, mostly from recent exposure; talk to a doctor about it.

This is not medical advice.
